# 1. Loading and processing gates from manual gating

```{r setup, results=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(IMPACD)
# devtools::build_vignettes() 
# devtools::load_all()
# devtools::document()
```

After loading `IMPACD`, start by loading the gate definitions from manual gating for your markers of interest.
Most times this gating step will be done in flowJo, but you could also gate in R or any other tool.
`IMPACD` supports most of the common gates, such as rectangular, polygon, threshold, and all kinds of logical gates.
You might store your gate defintions in a spreadsheet or a `.csv` file and load them, but in order for `IMPACD` to function, the resulting data table has to have four columns `Annotation`, `Name`, `Marker Type` and `Gate Position`:
```{r load gating data}
data(gate_definitions)
head(gate_definitions)
```

Here are logical gates, exported from flowJo:
```{r show logical gate}
tail(gate_definitions)
```

Important to note is that the coordinates will usually be in the untransformed space. For best results, we need to transfer them into the same space that the gating was initially done in. `IMPACD` can take care of this, but we will have to tell it what the transformations for each marker are. Transformations must be stored in a `transformList` object.

```{r load transformations}
data(transList_wsp)

# One way to extract transformations from the flowJo workspace file is:
# ws = open_flowjo_xml("path/to/flowJo_workspace.wsp")
# gs_flowJo = flowjo_to_gatingset(ws)
# trans = gh_get_transformations(gs_flowJo[[1]])
# transList_wsp = transformList(from = names(trans), trans)

```

With this, we can now ask `IMPACD` to process the table with gates. The `processGates` functions returns a list.
The first entry is a data frame that lists all the gates that were created and contains useful information on the types of gate, the positions in transformed space, and all kinds of subgates that are required for logical gates. The second entry contains the actual gate objects that will later be applied to the flow data.
```{r process gates}
output = processGates(gate_definitions, transList_wsp) 

gate_data = output[[1]]
head(gate_data)
gates = output[[2]]
```

# 2. Create gating set
Next, we need to load the fcs files, transform them into the same space as the initial gating was done in (and the gates have been defined in) and turn them into a gating set. Since `IMPACD` is usually done after some manual gating, the fcs files we are going to work with here, have already been cleaned and compensated. Additionally, the data has already been gate to contain only contain CD4+ cells. For these steps, we are relying on functionality from other packages like `flowCore` and `flowWorkspace`.

```{r load fcs files and transform}
# Within this vignette, we can directly load the flowSet
data(fs)

# Or you can manually construct the same flow set using the following
# fcsDir = system.file("extdata", package="IMPACD")
# fcsFiles = list.files(fcsDir, full = TRUE, pattern = "*.fcs")

# Turn into a flowSet
# fs = read.flowSet(fcsFiles)

# Apply transformation
for (fcs_ in names(fs@frames)) {
  fs@frames[[fcs_]] = flowCore::transform(fs@frames[[fcs_]], transList_wsp)
}
 
# Turn flow set into a gating set
gs = GatingSet(fs)
```

For later steps, we need to provide some kind of annotation. The annotation should be a data frame with columns `sampleName` and `condition` at a minimum.

```{r load annotation}
data(annotation)
annotation
```
# 3. Root path gating
In most cases `IMPACD` gets applied to a specific subset. In this vignette we are only interested in central memory (CM) effector T cells (Teff). Using the gate defintions that we provided, we can filter for the Teff CM cells with `Teff+/CD45RO+/TEM+`. In the language of `IMPACD` this is known as the root path and we can add the Teff CM population to our gating set with
```{r root path gating}
# Root path we want to gate for
root_path = "Teff+/CD45RO+/TEM+"

starting_node = "root" # root is the starting node in the fcs files "all cells"

root_node = rootLevelGating(gs, root_path, gate_data, gates, starting_node)
root_node
```
The root path gets applied to `gs` (which is a pointer and therefore is not returned) and we can now continue with `IMPACD` on only the Teff CM cells.

# 4. Stage 1 gating
After we have decided on a specific cell subtype (Teff CM) we can do what `IMPACD` refers to as stage 1 gating.
q> give a description of level 1 gating here.

For this example we are going to use all of the 1D positive gates from the gating definitions, except for `CD4+`.
```{r stage 1 gating}
# Pick gates
level1_nodes = gate_definitions$Annotation[1:22]
level1_nodes = level1_nodes[level1_nodes != "CD4"]
level1_nodes = paste0(level1_nodes, "+")
level1_nodes

# Apply stage 1 gating
level1_paths = level1Gating(gs, level1_nodes, gate_data, gates, root_node) 
```
The function `level1Gating` returns a dataframe that contains information about each level 1 node that was gated for, such as the node name, the parent population and others.
```{r explore level1_paths}
level1_paths
```
This can be used to extract cell populations from the gating set using functionality from `flowWorkspace`:
```{r get cell counts from stage 1}
counts = gs_pop_get_count_fast(gs, format = "long")

# Add percent parent
counts$PercentParent = counts$Count/counts$ParentCount*100

# Filter down to populations from stage 1 gating
counts = dplyr::filter(counts, Population %in% level1_paths$gs_path)
head(counts)

```

The `counts` object is a data frame that contains population counts for each node for each sample.

In the next step, we can ask `IMPACD` to calculate log2 fold changes and p values for differences between the "Control" vs the "Type 1 Diabetes" and "DSRegistry" groups

```{r analyse stage 1 results, message=FALSE, results=FALSE}
# Merge the annotation data into the counts frame
counts = merge(counts, annotation, by.x = "name", by.y = "fcsName")

summary = summarizePopulations(counts)
stats = generateStatistics(counts, summary, "Control", c("Type 1 Diabetes", "DSRegistry"))
```
In order to exclude false positives, the results should be adjusted:

```{r fdr adjust stage 1 results}
stats$fdr[stats$condition == "DSRegistry"] = p.adjust(stats$pvalue[stats$condition == "DSRegistry"], method = "BH")

stats$fdr[stats$condition == "Type 1 Diabetes"] = p.adjust(stats$pvalue[stats$condition == "Type 1 Diabetes"], method = "BH")

head(stats)
```

Unfortunately, none of the results are significant with FDR adjusted p-values < 0.05. The reason for that is that we only used a very small data set. So, for the sake of demonstration, we will consider everything with an adjusted p-value of < 0.5 as significant.

`IMPACD` comes with a function that can add columns that break out information about gating. This additional information can be very useful in downstream analysis, and is provided by `processGatingPaths`. The parameter `max_depth` tells the function how deep we gated after the root path.

```{r}
stats = processGatingPaths(stats, max_depth = 1)

head(stats)
```

For visualization, we can make a volcano-like plot for each population:
```{r volcano plots stage 1, fig.width=7, fig.height=5, fig.align = 'center'}
gg_vp_stage1 = stats %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = log2Fold, y = -log10(fdr), color = terminal_node)) + 
  geom_point(alpha=0.7, size=2.5, shape = 19) +
  facet_grid(. ~ condition, scales = "fixed") + 
  theme_bw()
  
gg_vp_stage1

```

We can also visualize the cell counts for the populations with adjusted p-values < 0.5

```{r stage 1 boxplots, fig.width=7, fig.height=5, fig.align = 'center'}
# pick only populations with significant fdrs in at least one of the experimental groups
stats_significant = dplyr::filter(stats, fdr < 0.5) 

# process the gating paths
counts = processGatingPaths(counts, max_depth = 1)

gg_box_stage1 = counts %>% 
    dplyr::filter(Population %in% stats_significant$path) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = condition, y = PercentParent, fill = condition) ) +
    geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
    geom_jitter(aes(color = condition), position = position_jitter(0.15)) +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_blank()) + 
    ylab("Percent of parent population") + 
    facet_wrap(.~ terminal_node, scales = "free", ncol = 3)

gg_box_stage1
```

For processing or sharing results outside of `R` it, the data frames can be written to csv files with `write.csv(stats_significant, file = "significant_results.csv")`.

# 5. Stage 2 gating
In stage 2, IMPACD performs exhaustive permutational analysis of all markers. This resembles what we just did for stage 1, but instead of stopping after the first node, in stage 2 we will keep adding more and more nodes until a specified depth is reached.
There are a few important considerations to consider on the way:
  - What should be the maximum depth?
  This depends on your data and the questions you try to answer. After adding 2 or 3 nodes, the information content that is added by gating deeper, usually drops. A maximum gating depth of three is usually recommended.
  - How many different nodes can I add?
  Keep in mind that IMPACD is exploring the full permutational space. That means if you have 10 markers (A, B, C,...), each of which can be positive or negative (A+, A-, B+, B-, C+, ...) and you chain them together in all possible ways, you will quickly end up with hundred of thousands of possible cell populations.
  
For this vignette, we will use only the first 10 nodes from the gate defintions. 
```{r stage 2 gating setup}
level2_nodes = gate_definitions$Annotation[1:10]
level2_nodes = c(paste0(level2_nodes, "+"), paste0(level2_nodes, "-"))
level2_nodes
```
Additionally, we need to provide `level2Gating` with the `root_node`, and a maximum gating depth. ```
An optional argument is `cellcountCutoff`. If the number of total cells for a given population across all samples is smaller than the value provided here, the subpopulation will be excluded from consecutive gating steps, saving computational resources.
```{r stage 2 gating}
level2_results = level2Gating(gs, level2_nodes, gate_data, gates,
                                starting_node = root_node,
                                max_depth = 3,
                                cellcountCutoff = 10)
```

This step might take a while to complete. The above gating approach gives >3000 subpopulation. We can run the same steps as before to generate summary statistics, and (adjusted) p-values.

```{r stage 2 counts}
# Extract counts from gating set
counts = gs_pop_get_count_fast(gs, format = "long")

# Add percent parent
counts$PercentParent = counts$Count/counts$ParentCount*100

# Add meta data
counts = merge(counts, annotation, by.x = "name", by.y = "fcsName")

# Generate summary statistics
summary = summarizePopulations(counts)
```

Before generating `logFC` and `p-values`, we should clean up the summary table. For example, we might not be interested in cell populations that don't have at least 20 cells total in at least one of the study groups. And we are also not interested in any of the populations from subgates from logical gates (OR). This can be accomplished with `cleanPopulations`.

```{r clean stage 2 pops}
# Number of unique populations before cleanup
print(length(unique(summary$path)))

summary = cleanPopulations(summary, minCellCount = 20, maxDepth = 3)

# Number of unique populations after cleanup
print(length(unique(summary$path)))
```
After a first clean up  pass, we can now calculate p-values:

```{r stage 2 stats, message=FALSE, results=FALSE}
stats = generateStatistics(counts, summary, "Control", c("Type 1 Diabetes", "DSRegistry"))

stats$fdr[stats$condition == "DSRegistry"] = p.adjust(stats$pvalue[stats$condition == "DSRegistry"], method = "BH")

stats$fdr[stats$condition == "Type 1 Diabetes"] = p.adjust(stats$pvalue[stats$condition == "Type 1 Diabetes"], method = "BH")
```
And add some more information about the gating:

```{r stage 2 gating paths}
stats = processGatingPaths(stats, max_depth = 3)

colnames(stats)
```
As you can see, this time we ended up with two additional columns "modifier_1" and "modifier_2". These will be used in the next step.

To help identify potentially interesting subpopulations `IMPACD` provides the `modifierAnalysis` function. 

>q Describe modifier analysis here

```{r modifier analysis}

report = modifierAnalysis(stats, counts, summary, "DSRegistry", p_cutoff = 0.1)

head(report)

```

This step significantly reduced the number of populations that are being reported. Note that `modifierAnalysis` returns all populations that had a not-adjusted p-value of `< p_cutoff`. You might need to filter the results further down to significant adjusted p-values.
The cell populations that we end up with after the modifier analysis step can now be used as starting point for any further down stream analysis or written to a csv file with `write.csv(report, file = "modifier_analysis_results.csv")`.
